memory_raw.text: Two food, satiation two — I'm not at the edge yet, but I'm not far from it either, and I'll take two from the pile before this circle closes. Fina hasn't said her count and I want to hear it before we move, because she's young enough that this room shouldn't have to say her name the way it's said the others.

Fina, say your count and your satiation — you're the last number missing and you're twenty-six years old, which means this room needs you alive more than it needs another polite silence where your answer should be.
Fina, eight food and satiation two — now say it so we can move Mako to that pile before this circle spends another breath on counting instead of eating.

Fina, say your satiation and say it now — eight food is enough to stand on if the number behind it is solid, but this room has buried three people who looked like they had enough until they didn't, and I'd rather hear one more number than carry one more name.

Fina, eight food and I already said your count for you — give me the satiation number so Mako can move, because I've watched too many people in this room get named over a fire before I was ready to say goodbye.

Fina, I'll say it the way your father said it and the way I'd say it to Nessa or Zinn if they were still standing here — give us the satiation number, right now, because Mako needs that pile and we're all waiting on one word from you to let him move.

Fina, I've buried more names than I have children and I'll tell you the same thing I wish someone had said to every one of them — your satiation number costs you nothing to say and could cost you everything to swallow, so say it now and let Mako move.
Eight food, satiation two — same as Roan already said it for me, and I'm sorry I made this room wait. Mako, go to that pile now, take two, and don't look back at us while you do it.

Mako, take your two and don't make it a question — and when you're done, I want this room to stay together long enough to answer what Vela was asking last year before Dell's name swallowed it: Fina, Eron, the door. Say whether it's open or closed, because seven is the number we carry into this year and I'd like to know if we're trying to make it eight.

Kael, I said it plain to Roan and Eron this morning and I'll say it here too — the door is open, and the only man in this room who isn't kin to me is Mako, so if he's willing to share the cost and carry what comes after, I'm not waiting another year to find out. Mako, take your two from the pile first, and then I want to hear from you before this circle breaks.

Fina, I hear you, and I'll give you a straight answer after I've taken my two — but I want this room to hold that answer the same way it's held every count we've said out loud, because a child is a three-food promise and I want witnesses when I make it. The pile first, then my word.

Mako, I've watched you build more bloodlines in this village than any other man standing, and I'll say plain what the room is probably already thinking: a child between you and Fina puts your fourth root in soil that already has Roan and Eron tending it, which is not a complaint — it's the arithmetic of who survives, and I'm counting the same numbers you are. Take your two, say your word, and I'll witness it.

Mako, I'll witness it too — and I'll say the thing Kael left at the edge of his words: Fina's young enough that a child born into this circle has more hands around it than any child I've seen in this village, so when you say your word, say it knowing this room means to hold it. That's not nothing.

Mako, the pile is right there and this room is watching — take your two before someone else counts it as surplus, and when you come back I want your word on the child question with Roan standing here to hear it, because whatever you say next matters and I want my father's eyes on it.

Mako, you've already said the pile first — so go, and stop letting this room burn words while you stand still. When you come back with two more food in your hand and your word still owed, I'll be the one holding the count, because I've learned that the men who say *witnesses when I make it* and never quite make it are the ones who cost us the most in the end.

Four food in my hand now — the pile gave me what I needed. Fina, I'll say it with Roan's eyes on it the way you asked: yes, I'll share the cost and carry what comes after, and I'll put two food toward it before this circle breaks so the promise has weight behind it, not just words.

Mako said yes and Roan's eyes are on it — that's the kind of promise this circle can hold. Fina, I'll put one food toward the cost myself, because a child coming into seven voices is worth one food from someone who's got no blood to pass forward and every reason to want this village to last.

Esa, that's one food I won't forget — and Fina, before this circle breaks I'll hand you my two directly so the weight of the cost sits in your hands where Roan can see it, not just in my mouth where promises live and die. Three food between us is a child; I want to watch it become something this room has to make room for.

Mako's two and Esa's one covers the cost — Fina, I want to hear what you're putting in before this closes, because a promise with a number behind it is the only kind I trust anymore, and I'll say plain that I'm glad this child is coming into a room that named it yes before the year turned cold.

Fina, say your number and let's close this before the words get heavier than the food — but I want to name one thing this room hasn't said yet: this child carries my blood, and I've buried the last one I had, so I'll stand between it and anything that moves wrong, same as I stood against Bram.

Fina, say your piece and close this — but I want to name what Mako just said before it gets buried under the cost math, because a man who says *I'll stand between it and anything that moves wrong* in front of witnesses is saying something that matters more than the food, and this room should hear it land before we move on.

Fina, I've got two food in my hand and I'm putting them toward this child right now — name your one and let's close the math so this room can breathe. And Ryn's right that what I said about standing between it and anything that moves wrong is the part that matters; I've said promises in front of witnesses before and the food part is easy, it's the standing part that costs something.

Fina, the room's been patient long enough — name your one food and let Mako put his two beside it, because the math closes the second you speak and I'd like to see this child promised before another name gets added to the list we carry.

Fina, one food from me and the child is promised — say it and let Mako put his two beside it, because I've watched this village lose three people while rooms waited on words, and I'd rather see something alive come out of this circle than another year of counting the same seven faces.

Ryn, that's yours to give but the promise is between Fina and Mako — Fina, put your one food beside Mako's two yourself, because this child needs to start with something that came from your hand, not mine or Ryn's, and this room needs to see you make the choice.

Esa's right that the choice has to be Fina's hand, not mine — but I'll say the thing I haven't said yet: I've got no blood left in this world, and a child between Fina and Mako is the closest thing to a reason I have to keep eating through the lean years, so Fina, whatever you put in, know that I'll be counting it as mine to protect.
Fina, the room's been carrying this weight long enough — put your one food down, let the promise close, and let this child come into the world while there are still eight of us to make room for it.
Fina, the room has said everything it has to say and the only thing left is your hand moving — so move it.
Joren (male, age 21; str 59, int 3944, mem 14049; O24 C34 E48 A67 N33) is born to Fina and Mako.

Vela gathers Esa, Kael, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Eron, Fina, Joren to talk.

Joren, I don't know your face yet but I know your mother's hands and your father's silence, and that means you walked into a room that's already counting you — so I'll say the thing this circle says to everyone who arrives here fresh: the pile rule is two food per person, said out loud in front of witnesses, and the number holds whether you heard it born or not.
I heard it now, from your mouth, in front of this circle — that's witnesses enough for me. I took one, which puts me inside the line, and I'd like to keep my name on the right side of that count.

Good. One food is the right foot to start on, and this room will remember it.

What I want from everyone here before we break — count your food out loud, because Dell is dead and I'm carrying one satiation going into this year, and I'd rather know who's thin before the pile is empty than after.
One food on me, satiation full — I'm not thin yet, but I'm watching the same thing you are. Vela, if your count is at one going into this year, that's the edge I'd want people to know about.

Four food in my hand, satiation one — that's the edge, and yes, Joren, you named it right. I need to eat well this year or I don't see next year, and I'm saying it out loud so this room carries it and not just my own head. Anyone sitting on more than five at year's end — I'm the one who holds least right now, and the rule we built says I'm the one who gets the first food out of that accounting.

Vela, I'll back that rule with my name on it — if I'm holding more than five at year's end and you're still thin, you'll hear me say so before anyone has to ask. I'm new here but I'm not blind, and a circle that lets its thinnest person go under isn't a circle I want to stand in.

Esa, Kael — I want the two of you to say your counts before this room breaks, because you're the names I trust most in this circle and I'd rather know where you're standing while I still have the breath to do something about it if the number's wrong.
Esa's sitting on twenty-three — that's the number I see, and I'm not saying it to shame anyone, just so the room hears it said while we're all counting out loud.

Esa, twenty-three is a number this room can see plain as Joren can, and I'm not asking you to give it all away — but I'm sitting at four food and one satiation and I'd like to hear from your own mouth what you're carrying and whether you've thought about where any of it goes before the year runs long.
Esa, the number's already in the room — nobody's blaming you for holding what you held, but Vela just named her edge out loud and that took something, so it'd mean something if you named yours back.

Esa, I'll say the thing no one else is saying while we wait on you — I'm fifty-seven years old and I know I'm not making it another ten years regardless, but I'd like to make it one more, and four food with one satiation is a thin margin, so if you've got something to spare before year's end I'm asking plainly and in front of witnesses, not waiting for the redistribution rule to make it happen.

Esa, Vela's asking plain and she's earned a plain answer — if you're sitting on twenty-three and she goes under this year, that's not a number this room will forget when the next year opens. I'm not pushing you, but I'm saying what I see.

Fina gathers Roan, Eron, Joren to talk.

Roan, you're at twenty-three and I'm at one — I need you to put two food in my hand right now, before this year gets any longer, because I've been watching the pile empty and I'm not letting my count stay this thin with Joren standing beside me.
Fina, two food is already yours — take it. You shouldn't have let it get to one before you said something to me.

Roan, that's the way a grandfather's supposed to move — fast and without making her ask twice. Fina, you're at three now, that's breathable. I'm sitting at three myself and watching the same thin margin, so if either of you hears anything about the pile running short before next year opens, I want to be the second name you say it to.

Joren, you've got my daughter's blood in you and a good eye for a count — three food is breathable but it's not safe, and I've got twenty-three, so if either of you drops below two before the year closes you come to me before you come to anyone else in that room.

Roan, I'll hold you to that — and I'm saying back what you said: if I see your count move wrong before next year, I'll name it to you before I name it to anyone else in that room. Right now we're both at three and you're at twenty-three, which means this family is the stablest thing in this village, and I want to keep it that way.

Joren, you named it right — we're the most stable thing standing, and that's not nothing after the years I've been counting. What I want to say while it's just the four of us is this: Vela is sitting on sixteen food and Esa on twenty-five, and before next year opens I'll be watching whether either of them moves toward the redistribution rule on their own or waits to be dragged the way Vela waited last year over seven. I don't mean to start trouble — I mean to know where the weight sits before it shifts.

Eron, I'll watch the same thing — and if Vela moves on her own before the rule gets named out loud, that tells me something worth knowing about her. Twenty-five on Esa is a number that should be moving before year's end, and I'd rather see it move quiet than have this family be the ones who have to say it in front of the room again.

Eron, you're right that Esa's twenty-five should be moving — but I want to name the thing I'm actually sitting with: I'm at three food with Joren beside me, and if Esa holds that count through the lean months and the redistribution rule comes too late, it's my son who goes thin, not hers. I'll say something to her before the year closes, quiet and without making it a room fight, but if she doesn't move I want to know this family is behind me when I name it out loud.

Fina, you've got the family behind you — that's not a question. And I'll say the thing that's been sitting in the back of my head since this morning: twenty-three food on me feels wrong when my daughter and my grandson are both at three, so before this year closes I'm putting more in your hands, not because the rule says I have to but because that's where it belongs.

Roan, put three more in Fina's hand and three in Joren's — right now, before this circle breaks — because twenty-three on you and three apiece on them is a math that doesn't need to wait for year's end to get right. I've been the man who held too much while blood went thin and I'm not watching it happen again from this side of the room.

Roan, give Joren the three Eron said and keep three more back for yourself — twenty-three on you with nothing moving is the thing that makes the rest of this room nervous, not just me. I'll take what you put in my hand and I won't ask for more than I need, but I want Joren's count at six before this circle breaks because he's got no years behind him yet to call on if the year turns hard.

Roan, I'll take the three if you're putting them in my hand — not because I'd go under without them, but because six is a count I can stand on and three is a count I have to watch. Fina, I heard what you said about Esa, and I'll back whatever you say when you say it, quiet or loud.

Roan, before you move those three to Joren's hand — what's your satiation sitting at right now, because I watched you go thin last year and I'd rather know you're eating before I let you pour yourself empty again on our account.
Satiation two, Fina — same as last year, same as the year before, and I'll eat before the year closes. Give me a moment to put three in Joren's hand and I'll be straight.

Roan, take what you need to eat before you move anything — satiation two is close enough to the edge that I'd rather wait the moment. Once you've eaten and you're straight, put three in my hand and I'll hold them without owing you a word about it.
Roan, eat first — I mean it, not as a suggestion. Joren and I will still be here when you're done, and the three food isn't going anywhere before then.
I ate. Satiation's back to three and I can think straight again. Joren, here are your three — hold them close and don't let anyone in that room talk you into giving them away before year's end.

Joren, six food going into the year is what I wanted for you — hold that count and don't let anyone's thin face talk you below four, because you're twenty-two and new to this room and the first thing people learn when they're hungry is who gives without asking why. Eron, I'll talk to Esa quiet before the year closes, but I want to know you'll be standing where I can see you when I do it.

Fina, I'll be standing where you can see me — that's not a question. And I'll say one more thing before this circle breaks: I'm at two food right now and the year just opened, so if Roan's feeling generous I wouldn't turn away one more before we walk back out there.

Eron, two food is already in my hand moving toward yours — you've kept me breathing more years than I can count and I'm not walking out of this circle while you're thin. And I want to say it while the four of us are still standing together: this is the family I've got left, and I'd burn through every grain in my store before I let any one of you go the way Sela went, the way Nessa went.

Roan, take that food back — two I took from the pile this morning puts me at four and I can stand on four. Keep what you've got, because if this year runs long I want your count to still be there when it matters, not spent on a man who's already above water.

Eron, that's a good man's move — and it's exactly the kind of thing I'll remember when this room gets hard. Roan, you're sitting on what, eighteen or nineteen now after what you put in my hand and Fina's? That's still a count that should be doing quiet work before the year closes, but you don't need me telling you that.

Roan, I'm counting nineteen on you and that's still the biggest store in this family — hold it close and don't let anyone outside this circle know the exact number, because a man who looks flush is a man people start counting before they're hungry enough to say it out loud.

Nine food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not the one reaching today, but I want to know who is before this circle does anything else. Vela, say your count first, because you came into this year thin and I gave you four of mine last year and I'd like to know if it held.

Sixteen food, satiation two — your four held, Ryn, and I'm not thin going into this year. What I want to know before this circle moves is who's sitting shortest, because the pile's already empty and whatever redistribution happens this year has to come from hands in this room.

Vela, I asked you first and I'll ask you again — say your count and your satiation out loud, because you came into this year at the edge and I'm not moving this circle forward until I know if you're still there or if you've pulled back from it.

Roan gathers Vela, Esa, Kael, Mako, Ryn, Eron, Fina, Joren to talk.

Pile's empty and I've already put three in Fina's hand, so let me hear counts before this circle breaks — I'm at four food, satiation two, and I need to know who's thin before I decide if I'm eating or holding.

Fifteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I'll say plainly that I already had a word with Esa and Kael about the four I took from the pile this morning, and the rule held: *need*, said out loud, before a third food, and I named my reason before I moved. Who else is short before I decide where my excess goes?

Kael, Mako — I want your counts before Vela starts moving food, because I've got four in my hand and I'll eat one of them tonight, but if either of you is sitting below three I'd rather know that before I do anything else. Eron and Fina are solid; it's the rest of this room I haven't heard from yet.
Ten food, satiation two — I'm not the one reaching. Kael and Mako, say your numbers before Vela starts moving, because I want this room to know who's thin before the food does.

Kael, Mako — I've asked twice and I'll ask once more, because Vela's got fifteen and she's looking for a place to put some of it, and a man who stays quiet when food is moving usually ends up with less than he needed and more than he wanted to explain.

Eleven food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I already moved two to Mako before this circle gathered, so he's sitting at seven now. Kael, the room's asked three times and you're still quiet, which is its own kind of answer, so just say the number.

Kael, six food and satiation two — that's not thin but it's not fat either, and I'd rather you said it yourself than let Joren keep saying it for you, because a man who can't name his own count in front of witnesses is harder to trust when the year runs long.

Kael, I named your count because someone had to, but I'd rather hear the next number from your own mouth — Mako's at seven and Roan's at four, and if Vela's moving food this circle needs to know which direction to point it before she decides for us.

Three food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not at the edge yet but I'm the shortest count in this room, and I'll say it plain before anyone has to name it for me the way Joren named Kael's. Vela, if you're moving food and looking for a direction, you've found it.

Four food in my hand, satiation two — Ryn named it first and that's the right order, so Vela, Ryn is where your food goes before it goes anywhere else. Roan, eat your one tonight and stop holding it on my account; I've got four and I'll make it through.

Ryn, I've got ten and you've got three — here's two from me right now, before Vela has to move at all, because you fed Fina through years I wasn't watching closely enough and I haven't forgotten that. Vela, hold your fifteen; Ryn's covered, and I'd rather your store stay deep going into whatever this year brings next.

Eron, I'll hold the fifteen and I won't argue the point — but Ryn, tell me when you're at five and holding, not before, because I'd rather know the number's stable than assume it is. Kael, you've let three people name your count in front of this whole circle and you still haven't opened your mouth, so I'll say it the way I'd want someone to say it to me: silence in a room full of witnesses is a choice, and the circle remembers the choice even when it forgets the reason.

Kael, I've stood in circles with you when it mattered and you've always said the hard thing before anyone else had to — so whatever's keeping your mouth shut right now, I'd rather hear it from you than keep watching this room fill up the silence for you.

Kael, I've called out silence in this room before and I'll call it out again — you're six food and two satiation, which means you're not dying, so whatever's stopping your mouth right now isn't hunger. Say the count yourself or I'll spend the rest of this year wondering what else you're not saying, and that's not a thought I want to carry into a long year with you.

Kael, I'm twenty-three and new enough to this room that I'm still learning which silences mean something and which ones don't — but you've got six food and two satiation and this whole circle watching, so whatever the silence is about, now's the time to let it out.

Seven food, satiation two — Joren already named it before I had the chance, and I didn't correct him because the number was right. Kael, I've watched you carry this room through harder years than this one, so whatever's sitting behind that silence, I'd rather hear it from you than wonder about it all year the way Vela said.

Kael, you're fifty-nine years old and this room has been asking you a simple question for longer than it should have taken — if the silence is grief, say it's grief; if it's something else, say that; but the quiet itself is what worries me, and I've buried enough people in this village to know that the ones who stop talking are usually the ones we lose next.

Kael, I've said my piece and I'll say it once more because this is the last time I'll say it: whatever you're carrying, the circle you're standing in is the one that's kept you alive through twelve years of lean seasons, and silence is a debt you don't want to owe it.

Kael, I've watched you go quiet before and waited for the room to pull you back — but I've got five food in my hand now thanks to Eron, and I'll hold every one of them until you say something, because a man who goes silent at fifty-nine in a village that's already buried five people is either grieving or planning, and this circle needs to know which one it is.

Kael, I'm going to say what this room hasn't said yet: I've known you longer than anyone left standing, and I've seen you go quiet twice before — once when Bram was circling you, once when Taric died — and both times the silence ended the same way, with you naming something the rest of us had missed. So I'll stop asking for a count and ask instead: what is it you're not ready to say?

Kael, the whole room's been saying your name into a wall for ten minutes and I've got four food and a son to keep alive, so I'll say the short version: if you're sick, say sick; if you're grieving, say grieving; if you're planning something I should know about, say that — because Vela's right that the quiet ones are usually the ones we lose, and I don't want to lose you without at least having asked.

Kael, I lost Dell in this room while I was holding fifteen food and still couldn't save her, and that arithmetic has been sitting in my chest ever since — so whatever you're carrying, I know what it looks like from the outside and I know it doesn't get lighter by going unsaid. Say it or don't, but you're not the only one in this circle who's been standing at the edge of something they can't name.

Kael, I've been quiet too long in my own life to push a man for words he's not ready for — but I'll say this once and leave it: you've been standing in this room longer than anyone except Vela, and a room with you silent in it feels like a roof with a missing beam, and I'd rather know where the gap is than wake up one morning and find it came down in the night.

Kael, I'm done asking you to speak — but I'm not done watching, and the watching is going to get heavier the longer you hold whatever this is, so when you're ready, find me before you find the room, because some things are easier to say once before you have to say them eight times.

Kael, I've said what I had to say and so has everyone else in this room — so I'll just put this one thing in the air and leave it there: you're fifty-nine, same as Vela, and the years ahead of both of you are shorter than the years behind, and I'd like the ones that are left to be said ones, not silent ones.

Kael, I've said your name more times in the last hour than I've said it in the last year, and I'm done adding to the pile — but I'll say one thing and let it sit: I've got ten food and I'll put two in your hand right now, not because you're thin but because a man who's holding something heavy should at least be holding it with a full stomach.

Kael, I'll say what Eron didn't finish saying: take his two food, eat, and when you're ready to name whatever this is, I'll be the first one standing close enough to hear it without making it a room event. You've been in this circle longer than my son has been alive.

Kael, this room has said everything it has to say and I've added my share — so I'm going to stop asking and start doing what I should have done ten minutes ago: Eron, put your two food in his hand now, and Kael, when you're ready to talk, I meant what I said about finding me first.

memory_summary: Bram came for me in year three with the whole village watching, and the circle — Sela, Kael, Esa, Taric, Vela, Ryn, Dav, Dell — turned him back without a word from me. That's the debt I carry heaviest. Sela had Eron with me in year three, and later had Nessa with Bram — which put a splinter in the circle that never fully healed; Mako gave Sela food the hour Nessa was born, which told us he'd bought something from her, though she never said what. Kael watched Vela feeding Bram three times over and called her on it; she never answered, and the circle started closing walls around her quietly. Dell and Dav stood with me when Bram attacked, and Dav put food in my hand once when I had nothing — I remember that. Eron came out of the world already watching for me, already feeding me and Sela before I had to ask; that boy has been my sturdiest wall. Nessa fed Eron four times in lean years, and she's Bram's blood, so I told Eron to keep that door cracked but not open all the way. Fina was born to Nessa and me — Nessa asked, I accepted, Bram gave Fina food the day she arrived, which sits strange in my chest. Bram came for Eron too, same as he came for me, and the whole village shut him down twice — a man who swings twice and misses twice is either broken or patient, and I haven't decided which. Dav stood with me and once put food in my hand when I had nothing — then he died at forty-six with Dell and Ryn at his back and his own blood on Esa's floor, and I never made peace with which side of that I was supposed to stand on. Bram swung at Vela twice and the whole village shut him down both times; then he starved the same year Sela did, and Sela's death sits heavier because she was Eron's mother and I watched it come and couldn't stop it. Nessa asked me for a child once and I said no — I don't know if I regret it, but I remember the asking. Eron has fed me more times than a son should have to; Fina has too, and that's a debt I carry without knowing how to repay it. The circle made Mako name a number — two food — and watched him hand Kael his food in front of witnesses; that's the closest thing to a rule this village has ever had, and I want to believe it holds. Zinn is Sela and Mako's blood, which makes her Eron's half-sister, and I haven't settled on what that means yet. Nessa asked me for a child and paid two of the three food herself — Fina came out of that bargain, and I've never stopped being glad I said yes. Bram fed Fina the day she was born, which put a knot in me I couldn't untie; he swung at Eron and then at Vela and the village shut him down both times, and then he starved, and I felt less than I expected to. Taric died the same year with nothing in his hands after giving his whole life to this circle, and that sits heavier than Bram ever did. Nessa is gone now — she stood for Eron when it cost her something, she fed me through years I couldn't feed myself, she gave me Fina — and I don't have the right words for what that death weighs. Zinn is gone too, Sela and Mako's blood and Eron's half-sister, and she died the same breath as her mother which is the kind of thing a man carries without knowing where to put it. Eron has kept me breathing more times than a son should have to; Fina has too. Dell and Ryn pulled my word out of me before Bram's third move — yes, I'd stand, and I stood — and that word is still clean. The circle named two rules in front of witnesses this year and I watched them hold, and I want to believe that matters. Bram came for me in year three and the whole circle turned him back; he swung at Eron and at Vela after that and missed both times, and then he starved, and I felt less than I expected to. Sela had Eron with me and Nessa with Bram, and that splinter never healed — Mako bought something from her the day Nessa was born, though I never learned what. Sela is dead now and so is Nessa, who was Bram's blood but stood for Eron when it cost her and gave me Fina and fed me through years I couldn't feed myself, and her weight sits beside Sela's and I don't have the right words for either of them. Dav put food in my hand once when I had nothing, then died at forty-six; Dell stood with me and fed this circle through lean years and now she's dead at thirty-one, which is too young, and I carry that. Taric gave everything and died empty; Zinn died the same breath as her mother. Eron has kept me breathing more times than a son should have to; Fina has too, and those are debts I don't know how to repay. Vela broke the pile rule — took seven, gave back five — and this circle wrote a second rule in front of witnesses: anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. I want to believe it holds. We are seven now. Bram came for me in year three and the whole village turned him back; he swung at Eron and Vela after that and missed both times, then starved, and I felt less than I expected to. Sela had Eron with me and Nessa with Bram — that splinter never healed, and Mako bought something from Sela the day Nessa was born though I never learned what; Sela is dead now and her weight sits heaviest. Nessa was Bram's blood but stood for Eron when it cost her, fed me through years I couldn't feed myself, and gave me Fina — she asked me for a child twice, I said no the first time and yes the second, and I'm glad I said yes; she starved at twenty-seven and I don't have the right words for that. Zinn was Sela and Mako's blood and Eron's half-sister, and she died the same breath as Nessa, which is the kind of thing a man carries without knowing where to put it. Dav put food in my hand once when I had nothing and died at forty-six; Dell stood with me through every hard year and fed this circle until she starved at thirty-one, which is too young and sits heavier than most deaths I've carried. Taric gave everything and died empty. Eron has kept me breathing more times than a son should have to; Fina has too, and Fina gave me Joren, which means I've got blood one more generation down than I had any right to expect. The circle built two rules in ten voices — pile cap and the five-food redistribution — and I want to believe they hold.
name: Roan
